title: The Invention of the Bicycle
summary: The story of how the bicycle developed from a pedal-less wooden running machine into the safe, two-wheeled design people ride today.
poll: The invention of the safe, modern bicycle changed how ordinary people lived more than most other inventions of the 1800s.

versions.title: The Invention of the Bicycle
versions.text:
Long ago, there were no bikes. People just walked. Some rode animals too.

A man made the first bike. His name was Karl Drais. It had two wheels. It had no pedals! A rider sat on it. The rider pushed their feet on the ground. This made it go. It was like walking, but fast. People called this invention a running machine.

Later, bikes got pedals. The pedals were on the front wheel. But the wheels were hard. Every bump hurt a lot. People called this bike a boneshaker.

Next came a strange bike. One wheel was huge. One wheel was tiny. It was fast. But it was not safe. Riders fell off a lot.

A man named John Kemp Starley had a good idea. He made a new bike. Both wheels were the same size. A chain joined the pedals to the back wheel. This bike was much safer.

Then a man named John Boyd Dunlop had an idea too. He put air inside the tires. Now rides felt soft and smooth.

Riders could balance well on this bike. It let them go far on their own.

versions.title: The Invention of the Bicycle
versions.text:
Look far back in time. There were no bicycles at all. People just walked. Some rode animals too.

A German man built a strange machine. His name was Karl Drais. It had two wheels. It had no pedals at all! A rider sat on a wooden seat. The rider pushed their feet on the ground. This made it move. It was almost like walking. People called this invention a running machine. It was faster than walking.

Years later, bikes got pedals. The pedals were on the front wheel. But the wheels were hard and made of wood. Every little bump shook the rider hard. People gave it a funny name: the boneshaker.

Next came an odd bike. It had one huge front wheel. It had one tiny back wheel. It could go fast. But it was not safe at all. Riders sat high up, so a small bump could make them fall.

An English man named John Kemp Starley solved this problem. He built a bike with two wheels the same size. A chain linked the pedals to the back wheel. This clever bike was much easier to balance. It was also far safer to ride.

A little later, a man named John Boyd Dunlop had an idea. He filled rubber tires with air. Now rides felt smooth.

Soon, many people began riding bikes on their own.

versions.title: The Invention of the Bicycle
versions.text:
For a long time, most people traveled on foot. Some rode animals when they needed to get somewhere. There were no bicycles at all, until a clever German man changed transportation forever.

In 1817, a German man named Karl Drais built a strange machine. It had two wheels. It had no pedals at all. A rider sat on a wooden seat and pushed their feet against the ground. This let them glide along faster than they could walk alone. People called it a running machine. Curious crowds gathered in the streets just to watch this odd machine roll past.

About forty years later, a mechanic in France attached pedals to the front wheel of a similar machine. Riders no longer needed to touch the ground with their feet. But this early bike still rolled on hard wooden wheels wrapped in iron. Every bump in the road shook the rider's whole body. People gave the rough bike a fitting name: the boneshaker.

After the boneshaker came a tall bike known as the penny-farthing. It had one giant front wheel and one tiny back wheel. A single turn of the pedals could carry a rider much farther. It could move quickly, but it was far from safe. Riders sat high above the ground, and the smallest bump could send them tumbling down.

In 1885, an English man named John Kemp Starley solved this problem with a clever design called the safety bicycle. It used two wheels of equal size, with a metal chain connecting the pedals to the back wheel. This was far easier to balance and much safer than any bike before it.

A few years later, a Scottish man named John Boyd Dunlop had another bright idea. He filled rubber tires with air instead of solid rubber or wood. This cushioned every bump, making rides smoother and much more comfortable.

With a safer design and comfy tires, the bicycle became cheap transportation that gave ordinary people a new sense of independence.

versions.title: The Invention of the Bicycle
versions.text:
For a very long time, most people traveled on foot or on animals to reach a place far from home. No faster, affordable way of traveling existed yet. There were no bicycles until the early 1800s. Then a clever German inventor changed the entire history of personal transportation with one surprisingly simple idea.

In 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais built a strange two-wheeled machine. It had no pedals attached to it at all. A rider sat on a wooden seat between the two wheels and pushed their feet against the ground, almost like walking while seated on a bench. This let them glide along noticeably faster than they could ever walk alone. People called this early invention a running machine. Curious crowds often gathered in town streets just to watch the odd contraption roll past.

About forty years later, a skilled mechanic working in France attached pedals directly to the front wheel of a similar machine. Riders no longer needed to touch the ground with their feet at all while it rolled forward. However, this early bicycle still rolled along on hard wooden wheels wrapped tightly in iron bands. Every single bump shook the rider's entire body, since no cushioning softened the blow. People gave this rough, uncomfortable machine a fitting nickname: the boneshaker.

After the boneshaker came a towering bicycle known as the penny-farthing, named after two old coins of very different sizes. It had one giant front wheel and one tiny back wheel. A single turn of the pedals could carry a rider much farther down the road than earlier designs allowed. It could move surprisingly quickly for its era, but it was far from safe. Riders perched high above the ground on a narrow seat, where the smallest bump could send them tumbling down headfirst.

In 1885, an English inventor named John Kemp Starley finally solved this dangerous problem with a clever new design that people soon began calling the safety bicycle. His design used two wheels of equal size, with a sturdy metal chain connecting the pedals to the back wheel, very much like the bicycles that people still ride today. This innovation was far easier to balance and considerably safer to ride than any design before it.

A few years later, a Scottish inventor named John Boyd Dunlop had another bright idea while watching his young son struggle to ride a tricycle over rough cobblestones. He filled rubber tires with air instead of solid rubber or wood. This simple but brilliant change cushioned every bump, making rides smoother and far more comfortable for riders of every age.

With a safer frame and comfortable tires, the bicycle became an affordable, everyday form of transportation. It gave ordinary people, including many women who had rarely traveled alone before this time, a thrilling new sense of independence and the freedom to go wherever they pleased.

versions.title: The Invention of the Bicycle
versions.text:
For thousands of years, most people traveled only on foot or on the backs of animals. No faster, affordable way of traveling existed for ordinary families. There were no bicycles anywhere until the early 1800s. Then a clever German inventor produced an innovation that would eventually revolutionize personal transportation across the globe.

In 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais built an unusual two-wheeled apparatus. It had no pedals attached to it at all, a detail that often surprises students today. A rider sat on a wooden seat between the two wheels and pushed their feet firmly against the ground, almost as though walking while seated. This allowed them to glide along noticeably faster than they could ever walk alone. People called this early invention a running machine. Curious crowds often gathered in town streets to watch the odd contraption roll past.

About forty years later, a skilled mechanic working in France attached pedals directly to the front wheel of a similar apparatus. Riders no longer needed to touch the ground with their feet at all. However, this early bicycle still rolled along on hard wooden wheels wrapped tightly in iron bands. Every single bump shook the rider's entire body, since there was no cushioning to soften the blow. People gave this rough machine a fitting, if unflattering, nickname: the boneshaker.

After the boneshaker came a towering bicycle known as the penny-farthing. It had one giant front wheel and one tiny back wheel. A single turn of the pedals could propel a rider much farther down the road than earlier designs had allowed. It could move surprisingly quickly for its era, but it offered little real mobility to most riders. One perched dangerously high above the ground, where the smallest bump could send a rider tumbling headfirst onto the street below.

In 1885, an English inventor named John Kemp Starley finally solved this dangerous problem with a clever new design. People soon began calling it the safety bicycle, precisely because it was far less likely to cause injury. His design used two wheels of equal size, with a sturdy chain connecting the pedals to the rear wheel. This innovation proved far easier to balance and considerably safer to operate than any design before it.

A few years later, a Scottish inventor named John Boyd Dunlop had another bright idea while watching his son struggle to pedal a tricycle over rough cobblestones. He filled rubber tires with pneumatic pressure, pumping them full of ordinary air instead of building them from solid rubber or wood. This deceptively simple change cushioned every bump along the road, making rides smoother and far more comfortable for riders of every age.

With a safer frame and comfortable, pneumatic tires, the bicycle quickly became an affordable, everyday form of transportation. It gave ordinary people, including countless women who had rarely traveled alone before, a thrilling new sense of independence, personal mobility, and freedom.

A few years later, a Scottish inventor named John Boyd Dunlop had another bright idea while watching his young son struggle to pedal a tricycle over rough cobblestones near their home, and he filled rubber tires with pneumatic pressure, pumping them full of ordinary air instead of building them from solid rubber or carved wood, as every tire before his had always been laboriously constructed by hand. This deceptively simple innovation cushioned every bump along the road, making rides smoother, quieter, and far more comfortable for riders of every age and athletic ability, including children, working adults, and the elderly alike, almost overnight, across an entire continent.

With a far safer frame and comfortable, pneumatic tires, the bicycle quickly became an affordable, everyday form of transportation that gave ordinary people, including countless women who had rarely traveled alone before this era, a thrilling new sense of independence, personal mobility, and the freedom to go wherever they pleased, without needing anyone else's help, money, or permission to do so at all, ever again, for the rest of their lives.
